en: WASHINGTON — The U.S. State Department on Monday highlighted cooperation with South Korea and other partners on quantum technology, underscoring the importance of joint research, secure supply chains and international standards in the emerging strategic industry. The department's Bureau of Economic Affairs said in a post on X that Ambassador-at-Large for Cyberspace and Digital Policy Adam Cassady and Brad Blakestad of the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy led a U.S. delegation to the sixth Quantum Development Group (QDG) meeting held in South Korea. "Quantum will reshape how we secure communications, discover new medicines, and strengthen our economy. Who sets the rules matters," the department said. It said the U.S. delegation worked with trusted partners on research, supply chains and standards during the meeting, highlighting Washington's efforts to shape the global development of quantum technologies. "By investing in American ingenuity, the United States is making sure quantum breakthroughs strengthen our security, grow our economy, and create high-paying jobs at home," the department said. QDG is a U.S.-led international consultative body launched in July 2024 to promote the secure and responsible development and commercialization of quantum technologies. It comprises 13 countries, including South Korea, the U.S., Japan and Britain, and seeks to strengthen cooperation in research security, investment, supply chains and international standards

South Korea will help build a global "artificial intelligence (AI) basic society" in which no country is left behind in the AI transformation, the finance minister said Tuesday. Finance Minister Lee Hyoung-il made the remarks during a speech at the Global AI and Digital Summit, a three-day event co-hosted by the science ministry and the World Bank, which opened in Seoul on Tuesday. "South Korea, which received support from the international community as an aid recipient, has experienced how technology can transform the economy and people's lives during its development," Lee said. "South Korea wishes to become a partner for developing nations in their AI transformations, drawing on our experience and capabilities," he added. To this end, Lee said South Korea is working with six multilateral development banks, including the World Bank, to establish an AI hub bringing together their AI cooperation centers in South Korea. "The goal (of launching the hub) is to ensure no country or individual is excluded from the benefits of AI and to realize a global AI basic society," Lee added. The previous day, Lee met with Ajay Banga, president of the World Bank, to discuss ways to share South Korea's AI capabilities and experience with developing nations. The two exchanged views on using South Korea's nuclear energy technologies to secure a stable power supply and support sustainable growth in developing nations. They stressed the need to ensure industrial development that creates more opportunities and jobs for young people, and to continue efforts to promote inclusive and sustainable development in developing nations, according to the finance ministry. The Global AI and Digital Summit in Seoul, meanwhile, brought together around 900 participants, including relevant ministers and private-sector officials, from some 160 countries, making it the largest gathering since the World Bank launched the annual event in 2024, according to the finance ministry

Police said Tuesday they have arrested two people for their alleged involvement in a late-night mass brawl between Central Asian nationals in Pyeongtaek earlier this month. The brawl, involving 21 suspects, took place at around 11:40 p.m. on Oct. 3 at a children's park in the city, about 60 kilometers south of Seoul, raising safety concerns among residents. The Pyeongtaek Police Station said it caught five suspects allegedly involved in the brawl -- all of whom are Kazakh or Kyrgyz nationals in their 20s or 30s. It placed two of the five under arrest for alleged assault. Police officials have issued exit bans on two other suspects while investigating the whereabouts of 14 others. They believe the fight broke out over a past dispute and is unrelated to gang activity. Most of the suspects are believed to be day laborers, with three of the five apprehended suspects being undocumented migrants

Program offers practical Korean lessons, peer mentoring Sejong University said Sunday that its Sejong Korean Language and Culture Education Center, part of Daeyang Global College, completed a Campus Survival program last month to help newly enrolled international students adjust to university life in Korea. Held from Sept. 11-25, the program provided 408 international freshmen with practical Korean expressions and information about university life. It also gave them opportunities to interact with senior students. The program was selected as an outstanding initiative in a competition organized by the Ministry of Justice’s immigration integration division to promote early adaptation programs. The center ran the program in five sessions alongside the Campus Life Seminar, a required course for all newly enrolled international students. The sessions focused on helping students navigate everyday university life through practical information and useful Korean expressions. Five senior international students served as mentors, meeting with freshmen in small groups. They shared information on academic options and student support programs, including double majors, minors, self-designed majors, scholarships, extracurricular activity points and the university’s 1,000 won breakfast program. They also shared their university experiences and answered freshmen’s questions. “I remember how difficult it was to navigate university life when I first enrolled because I lacked information. I wanted to help new students, even in a small way, so I prepared for the program,” said Yusupova Odinabonu Sherzod Kizi, a student mentor. She also advised the freshmen on the importance of learning Korean, adapting to Korean culture and managing their studies. “I felt that my efforts had paid off because the students listened attentively and actively asked questions throughout the session,” she said. The center’s Clean Step plogging program was also recognized as an outstanding initiative in a social integration program competition. Through such initiatives, the center has continued to help international students develop a sense of belonging to the local community and build the skills needed to settle in Korea

Kim Ji-yong, the inaugural chief of the Serious Crime Investigation Agency (SCIA), attended a Cabinet meeting presided over by President Lee Jae Myung for the first time Tuesday, sparking controversy over the agency's political neutrality. Kim, who received his letter of appointment from Lee on Monday, was scheduled to hold his inauguration ceremony Tuesday afternoon. The SCIA was launched Oct. 2 as part of an overhaul of the criminal justice system that removed prosecutors' independent investigative powers. Kim emphasized the agency's political neutrality and independence before his appointment, saying he would decide whether to attend the Cabinet meeting after reviewing relevant laws and consulting with concerned agencies. Concerns have been raised that the participation of investigative agency and prosecution chiefs in Cabinet meetings could undermine their political neutrality and independence. In principle, even officials at the presidential office can be subject to investigation and prosecution, and holding weekly in-person meetings with the president itself could place political pressure on the agencies, critics say. In the past, the prosecutor general did not attend Cabinet meetings, but the practice changed early this year after Lee expanded participation to include the heads of government agencies, including the top prosecutor. Kim Jong-chul, acting commissioner general of the Korean National Police Agency, has also been attending Cabinet meetings, departing from the agency's previous practice. In a recent public statement, a local civic group, People's Solidarity for Participatory Democracy, voiced opposition to the practice, saying the political neutrality of investigative and prosecutorial authorities must be guaranteed

The Bank of Korea (BOK) said Tuesday it is expanding cooperation with the Bank of England (BoE) on tokenization projects. Sarah Breeden, the BoE's deputy governor for financial stability, visited the BOK on Monday and exchanged views with BOK officials on innovations in payment and settlement, according to the BOK. Breeden and other BoE officials shared updates on tokenization projects, including the global initiative Project Agora and South Korea's Project Hangang, with their BOK counterparts. The BOK said it will actively share its experience with tokenization projects and participate in global discussions on the matter. Payment tokenization is a security process that replaces sensitive payment data with a unique, randomly generated string of characters called a token. Project Agora, led by the Bank for International Settlements, explores how tokenized commercial bank deposits and tokenized wholesale central bank money can improve the global financial system, particularly cross-border payments. Project Hangang is a blockchain-based tokenization pilot project led by the BOK to test digital currency and wholesale central bank digital currency

FC Seoul’s 10-year wait for the K League title is almost over. The capital club was last champion of Korea in 2016, then a third triumph in six years. At the time, Seoul was a powerhouse of soccer in the Land of the Morning Calm and had the mighty goal machine Dejan Damjanovic in attack. The team was unlucky to lose the final of the Asian Champions League in 2013. The last decade has, however, been one to forget. Victory over Gangwon FC on Saturday will start the celebrations in front of the home fans at Seoul World Cup Stadium. It would be the perfect way to do it, for coach Kim Gi-dong to get the party started up by the banks of the Han River. Fans have been waiting for some time but this season looked different from the start. Seoul has been at the top of the standings from the get-go. At the moment, the club is 16 points clear with six games remaining. Only Ulsan HD can theoretically catch the leader but the Tigers will have to win all six (highly unlikely as the team has won just 15 of the 32 so far) and hope that Seoul does not manage a single victory. In short, it is 99.99 percent done. Seoul’s attack has been the standout, with 60 goals from the 32 games, nine more than any other. Coach Kim will be especially delighted that those goals are not just dependent on one attacker. Polish striker Patryk Klimala has 16 goals with Jeong Seung-won on eight, Lee Seung-mo has six with Song Min-gyu on five, a healthy spread. The defense has not been bad either. There is one negative to the season. Seoul has qualified for the AFC Champions League Two, the continent’s second-tier tournament. It does not have the stature or the profile of the Champions League Elite but Seoul has never won any continental trophy. So it was disappointing to see coach Kim rest most of his regular starters for the first two games in the group. It meant that Seoul lost to Indonesia’s Persib Bandung and then to Melbourne Victory all the way down in Australia. Coach Kim’s excuse was that he did not expect to be participating in the tournament at all and was surprised to qualify at the end of last season. The meaning is that the team was not capable of competing on two fronts. "We were not in a position to participate in the ACL this season,” he said after facing criticism for his rotation policy. “We ended up entering suddenly and hastily." He added that in the early part of the season, "we assembled a squad capable of focusing solely on the league. Once we qualified for the ACL, we were not in a position to recruit additional players." It means that Seoul is unlikely to finish in the top two in its group and a path to a first Asian trophy is already almost closed off. Kim’s excuse would have been better had Seoul not been so far ahead in the K League. The title has been in the bag for weeks meaning there was room to shift the focus toward Asia. Despite that, 2026 is going to be a historic season for FC Seoul as fans celebrate a long-awaited title. Even if it does not happen this weekend, it is only a matter of time

Lee's research focuses on chronic diseases, public health Lee Do-youn, a professor at Kookmin University’s College of General Education, has been named to the 2026 World’s Top 2% Scientists list jointly released by Stanford University and Elsevier. The list identifies the top 2 percent of researchers in their respective fields based on a comprehensive analysis of research impact, including citation metrics and research output, using data from Elsevier’s Scopus database. Kookmin University said Lee has broadened her research beyond physical therapy and rehabilitation science to encompass epidemiology and public health. Her research has focused on chronic diseases, major health risk factors, long-term trends in disease burden and the effectiveness of rehabilitation treatments. More recently, she has analyzed large-scale health care data from Korea and other countries to examine trends in disease incidence and prevalence, the burden of mortality and disability, and health disparities by age and gender. She also conducts evidence-based health care research by synthesizing and evaluating scientific evidence on various health issues to support disease prevention, treatment and health promotion. The research helps identify major health challenges associated with an aging population and provides empirical evidence to inform the development and improvement of health care policies. “I am honored to be named among the World’s Top 2% Scientists. This recognition reflects the collaborative efforts of colleagues in Korea and abroad. It is particularly meaningful to be able to contribute to Kookmin University’s growth as a world-class research university,” Lee said. “I am also grateful to the university for supporting my research. I will continue my efforts to ensure that my findings can be applied in clinical practice and public health policy,” she added. Lee’s research aligns with Kookmin University’s mid- to long-term development strategy, KMU VISION 2035: EDGE, launched as the university marks its 80th anniversary. EDGE stands for entrepreneurship, digital transformation, global competency and ESG (environmental, social and corporate governance). Guided by its vision of becoming “a university that sets the standard for higher education,” the university aims to expand interdisciplinary collaboration in education and research and strengthen its contributions to society

Samsung Bioepis has secured a decade-long exclusive supply deal for a rare disease treatment in Brazil, strengthening its position in Latin America’s largest pharmaceutical market while opening a new chapter in its partnership with the Brazilian government. The Korean biopharmaceutical company said Tuesday it had signed a local partnership agreement to supply SB12, a biosimilar of Soliris with the active ingredient eculizumab, to Brazil’s Ministry of Health. SB12 is used to treat rare conditions including paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria, a blood disorder, and atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome, which can damage blood cells, kidneys and other organs. Brazil’s health regulator, the National Health Surveillance Agency, known as ANVISA, approved the drug in December 2024. The Brazilian eculizumab market was worth about $170 million (250 billion won) last year, according to the company, which expects the 10-year exclusive supply agreement to provide a stable source of revenue. Under the government-led Productive Development Partnership program, Samsung Bioepis will work with Brazilian pharmaceutical company Bionovis and state-owned research institution Bahiafarma to supply the medicine and transfer technology to local partners during the contract period, which begins next year. The agreement expands Samsung Bioepis’ Brazilian portfolio to three products, building on supplies of SB4, a biosimilar of Enbrel, since 2019 and SB3, a biosimilar of Herceptin, since 2020. The company said cumulative shipments of the two existing products to Brazil have exceeded 6 million units, demonstrating its manufacturing and supply capabilities in the market. Jin-han Jung, executive vice president and head of Samsung Bioepis’ CS3 team, said the company would work with local partners to improve access to high-quality medicines for Brazilian patients with rare diseases and support the long-term development of the country’s biopharmaceutical industry. Brazil accounts for about half of Latin America’s pharmaceutical market, while its market for original biologic medicines reached 23 trillion won in 2024, according to the company. Works by American artist Lynn Hershman Leeson, a pioneer of media art, will be shown in Seoul in her first solo exhibition in Asia, the Seoul Museum of Art (SeMA) said Tuesday. Titled "Lynn Hershman Leeson: First Person Plural," the exhibition, which begins Wednesday, will bring together some 200 pieces of her work spanning painting, photography, sculpture and media installation, according to SeMA. Born in 1941, Leeson is known for experimenting with new technologies, such as video, the internet, artificial intelligence (AI) and genetic engineering, and transforming them into forms of art. In the 1970s, she carried out a multi-year performance art project in which she lived as Roberta Breitmore, a fictional alter ego she created. In the 1980s, she showcased the interactive work "Lorna," in which viewers can take part in an artwork by using a remote control to choose the narrative. The upcoming SeMA exhibition comprises six sections, which allow visitors to explore how born identities are expanded through social relationships, connected through media and network and undergo biological changes through genetic engineering, the museum said. For the exhibition in Korea, her interactive media artworks originally created in English, such as "Lorna," "Deep Contact" and "Agent Ruby," will be shown in Korean language for the first time. In an effort to highlight her career not only as a media artist, but also as a filmmaker, special screenings of her feature films, will be held in collaboration with the Seoul Art Cinema. The exhibition runs at the Seosomun branch of SeMA through Feb. 21

WASHINGTON — U.S. President Donald Trump on Monday expressed uncertainty about the possibility of meeting North Korean leader Kim Jong-un in China next month, saying he was not sure whether anyone had requested such a meeting. Trump made the remarks when asked by a reporter whether he expected to secure a meeting with Kim during his planned attendance at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in China, scheduled for November 18-19 in Shenzhen. "Oh, I don't know. I don't know," Trump said at the White House. "I'm not sure that anybody's asking for a meeting." The president nevertheless emphasized his personal ties with the North Korean leader. "I get along with him very well," Trump said. "But my relationship with Kim Jong-un is very good." In August, Trump said that he hoped to meet Kim later this year, adding to speculation that he might seek to rekindle his personal diplomacy with Kim that led to three bilateral in-person meetings: the first in Singapore in June 2018, the second in Hanoi in February 2019 and the third at the inter-Korean border village of Panmunjom. Last Monday, Trump said that he may meet Kim during his upcoming trip to Asia, adding, "That'll be exciting, won't it? But I get along with him." Tommy Pigott, spokesperson for the State Department, said earlier that Trump does not view talks with North Korea as a "concession" and is willing to engage Pyongyang if doing so serves U.S. national interests

North Chungcheong Province said Tuesday it will hold its annual cosmetics and beauty expo in Cheongju to help Korean companies expand exports of cosmetics and other beauty products. The Cosmetics & Beauty Expo Osong Korea 2026 will run from Thursday to Saturday in Osong, a district of Cheongju, 83 kilometers south of Seoul. The event aims to connect local companies with international buyers, according to the provincial government. "This year's expo, the largest edition to date, will provide local companies with opportunities to expand into overseas markets and allow visitors to experience K-beauty products," Jang Woo-sung, director general of the provincial government's bureau of biologics, food and drugs, said. The expo has been held annually in Cheongju since 2013, except in 2014. The provincial government has partnered with the Korea Trade-Investment Promotion Agency (KOTRA) to invite 200 domestic and international buyers, including representatives of Japanese retailer Ito-Yokado and Marui Group. The organizers expect the event to facilitate more than 1,200 one-on-one business meetings aimed at generating potential deals. The number of prominent overseas buyers is expected to rise to 26 this year from six last year, more than quadrupling, amid growing global demand for K-beauty products, according to the provincial government. Two seminars are also scheduled during the expo, including one organized by the French-Korean Chamber of Commerce and Industry (FKCCI) on strategies for entering European markets and another on next-generation cosmetics technologies

Enormous — and at times destructive — public demonstrations in France have significance reaching well beyond that historically turbulent nation. Protests began in September, spurred by deteriorating conditions in the education system. More than 500 schools have been blockaded and clashes with police have escalated to violence. In 2023, similar protests resulted from efforts by President Emmanuel Macron to increase the full retirement age in France. The initiative to raise the retirement age from 62 to 64 was successful but faces continuing opposition and pushback. The lower house was bypassed in the retirement reform. Macron has relied heavily on executive power rather than parliament. The constitution of the Fifth Republic, instituted by President Charles de Gaulle, defines a powerful chief executive. The massive displays of public hostility have added importance, given the central role of France in the European Union and the continuing war in Ukraine. Protestors set fire to trash bins in Paris. There has been sporadic fighting with police. Separate from the pension protests, protestors near the village of Sainte-Soline clashed with police over a projected water reservoir, which was opposed by environmentalists. These dramatic developments began only eleven months after Macron’s impressive reelection to office in April 2022. He received just over 58 percent of the vote, while his opponent Marie Le Pen received under 42 percent. This margin, while decisive, was narrower than in 2017 when these same two candidates competed for the presidency. The presidential elections seemed to indicate political stability of domestic institutions. However, the sustained protests reflect the growing difficulty in funding the welfare state. This is the harsh reality. The decisive, stunning military defeat of the large, well-armed but rigid and old-fashioned army of France in the spring of 1940 by the fast-moving German army started four years of humiliating occupation. Years of weak, ineffective governments followed the Allied liberation of France in 1944. General Charles de Gaulle, the exceptional leader of the Free French during the war, returned as leader of France in 1958. He succeeded in stabilizing the nation’s politics, and finally reestablished effective national authority and legitimacy. De Gaulle’s constitution creates a powerful presidency, which has been key to its long-term stability. A referendum in 1962 confirmed direct election of the president through universal suffrage. In 2000, a referendum reduced the presidential term from seven to five years. In this century, the alliance with the U.S. has been strong. Immediately after the terrorist attacks of 9/11, French aircraft joined those of other NATO allies in patrolling the skies over North America. The struggle against al Qaeda and other groups represents a comprehensive collective enterprise, authorized and supported by the United Nations as well as the NATO alliance. De Gaulle was in power during U.S. President Dwight Eisenhower’s second term. Eisenhower developed good working rapport with the difficult French leader during the second World War. While planning the Normandy invasion, some American and British air commanders argued against heavy bombing, which would unavoidably kill civilians. Eisenhower, then serving as the commander of the Allied Expeditionary Force, was able to turn to de Gaulle for support. The Kennedy and Johnson administrations clashed with de Gaulle’s nationalist rigidity. In 1966, France withdrew from NATO. Fortunately, in 2009 the nation rejoined the alliance. Today, astute support from allies could help stabilize France. Recent treaties with Britain and Germany might provide useful indirect leverage. That is the topic for a future column. Arthur I. Stars from the top U.S. and domestic women's golf tours will converge for an LPGA Tour event in South Korea this week, with a hometown favorite looking to defend her title. The LPGA Tour will bring its annual Asian swing to Haenam, some 330 kilometers south of Seoul in Jeonnam-Gwangju, for the BMW Ladies Championship at Pine Beach Golf Links. The 72-hole stroke-play tournament goes from Thursday to Sunday, with a total purse of $2.35 million. This will be the second straight edition of the tournament played in Haenam. Kim Sei-young, who is from the nearby town of Yeongam, won last year's tournament in front of dozens of friends and relatives to end a five-year LPGA title drought. At No. 9 with 13 career LPGA wins, Kim has had a strong 2026 season with seven top-10 finishes in 17 starts -- a run that will surely improve with a second straight BMW title on home soil this week. No player has won consecutive BMW tournaments since its launch in 2019. Kim is the third-highest ranked South Korean player in the field. World No. 3 Ryu Hae-ran leads all South Korean players in the rankings and will also be the highest-ranked player at this tournament. The 25-year-old has had a breakout campaign this year by winning two major titles and notching eight other top-10 finishes. Kim Hyo-joo, world No. 5, is also a two-time tour winner this year who has four other top-10 finishes. She will chase her career win No. 10, which would make her the sixth South Korean player to reach double figures in LPGA titles. This week will also see 15 players from the Korea LPGA (KLPGA) Tour, including its two best players this year -- Kim Min-sol and Seo Kyo-rim. Kim, a 20-year-old rookie, is leading the tour in money and the Rookie of the Year points. Kim is also second in the Player of the Year points, behind Seo, who is in second place on the money list. Seo has won four KLPGA tournaments this year to Kim's three. In the world rankings, Kim is the top KLPGA player at No. 13, with Seo checking in at No. 32. "I think you're going to have a tremendous victory, actually," Trump can be heard saying on speakerphone. "You're the man I want by my side, Bibi," Trump said, referring to Netanyahu by his nickname. Netanyahu — while reminding the famously loose-lipped president that they were on an open line — hailed Trump for joining Israel in attacking Iran in late February. "Donald, we have a job to finish," a beaming Netanyahu said. "We'll finish it together. We'll finish it, and no one else will do it." Netanyahu, Israel's longest-serving prime minister, had waited for years for a U.S. president who would agree to attack Iran. But Trump abruptly switched course in April and reached with Iran a ceasefire that is now in tatters. Polls showed that Trump's approval rating in Israel dropped sharply afterwards. David Makovsky, a fellow at the Washington Institute for Near East Policy, said it was unclear that Trump's endorsement would have a "huge impact" on Israelis. Netanyahu is "a polarising figure. You either love him or hate him," Makovsky said. "How many undecideds are there? Not that many." Trump went ahead with the endorsement despite open tensions involving top U.S. officials. WASHINGTON — The U.S.-Ukraine alliance is careening toward a possible breaking point, with Moscow strengthened by President Donald Trump's recent rejection of new Russia sanctions and Kyiv undermined by disruptions in satellite support for its drones during the war. Trump's relationship with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has always been a moving target , while the Republican president has frequently boasted of his rapport with Russian leader Vladimir Putin . But relations between the U.S. and Ukraine appear to be at a new low, threatening to tip the balance of the war to Russia's favor and imperil America's security interests across the globe. “At this moment in time, things look blacker than they ever had regarding this administration’s policy towards Russia and Ukraine,” said John Herbst, a former ambassador to Ukraine under President George W. Bush and now a scholar with the Atlantic Council. Trump has been lobbing insults at Zelenskyy for over a week and turning to policies that benefit Putin, while Ukraine's president has said he feels betrayed and worries for his country's future. But the American president can still shift on Zelenskyy — especially as he faces bipartisan outrage from lawmakers — which Trump has done before. Trump famously thrashed Ukraine’s leader in the Oval Office last year, warning him to “make a deal or we are out." Washington briefly suspended intelligence sharing. But Trump was praising Zelenskyy by that July and said they “actually developed a good relationship.” “Trump is a mercurial guy,” Herbst said. “He can wake up tomorrow morning, decide he’s done enough on this, and he might start to lean back in the other direction.” No one has taken responsibility for satellite restrictions on Ukraine Trump's recent decisions have baffled experts and infuriated Democrats and some Republicans ahead of pivotal midterm elections in two weeks. After The Wall Street Journal reported that Putin raised the prospect of a meeting with Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping to negotiate an end to the war in Ukraine , Trump told reporters Monday that he was open to it but expected it to focus on denuclearization efforts. Asked whether he would be willing to negotiate the end of the war without Zelenskyy, Trump appeared to indicate yes. “I think it’s time for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine,” Trump said. Trump decided Friday to waive sanctions on Russia in a bill that Congress overwhelmingly passed to support Ukraine. Named after late South Carolina Republican Sen. Lindsey Graham , the legislation targeted the flow of financial resources fueling Russia's war. That rebuke followed Trump's announcement of a deal to import Russian diesel fuel in a long-shot effort to curb high gas prices . The agreement was pilloried by Republicans and Democrats alike who say it will help Russia without making a difference in global fuel prices, which are elevated mostly due to Trump’s war against Iran. Then there were changes in SpaceX's satellite support to Ukraine's military, for which no one has taken responsibility. Starshield is a military-grade version of SpaceX’s Starlink satellite internet service and the backbone of Ukraine’s drone operations and communication. Zelenskyy says his country is facing major speed restrictions, so Ukrainian drones have been unable to intercept Russia's jet-powered drones. SpaceX chief Elon Musk, a Trump ally, has said Starshield is controlled by the U.S. and any limits are decided by the military and ultimately Trump. But Trump told reporters Friday that he did not order restrictions and doubted that Musk did either. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Saturday that Ukraine wants access to Starshield but doesn't have it. On Monday, he said the Pentagon controls Starshield, and "Ukraine has benefited from it” and wants to expand its use to conduct attacks beyond its territory. The U.S. military has not responded to questions about its involvement.

Before Jongno 3-ga claimed the top spot in Time Out's list of the " world’s coolest neighborhoods " in September, its bustling, vibrant streets filled with street food stalls and busy shops have long stood witness to its reputation as one of Seoul’s hippest hangout spots. But beyond this trendy landscape, photographer Park Kwang Bok’s attention gravitated towards the area’s more precarious yet intimate side. For his exhibitions titled “Earthly Paradise” and “Nights in Paradise” — both opening Tuesday — the artist explored the neighborhood’s gritty, hidden corners in search of narratives of joy, companionship and freedom. “Earthly Paradise” displays scenes of companionship and moments of happiness among the homeless despite their difficult circumstances. Featuring black-and-white photographs, the showcase seeks to “lift the veil of social prejudice and reveal the joy, tenderness and dignity that often go unnoticed.” Meanwhile, “Nights in Paradise” explores the lives of gay men who gather around Jongno 3-ga, portraying the community’s humanity, relationships, emotions and dignity. This latest exhibition series stemmed from his earlier 2018 documentary work, “Janggi Heaven,” in which he photographed elderly people playing “janggi,” or Korean chess, around Tapgol Park. During subsequent visits to Jongno 3-ga, his interest gradually shifted toward the area’s homeless community, with whom he formed friendships over time. “I saw moments when, despite living on the streets, they danced, smiled and found happiness. Rather than focusing on hardship and suffering as other photographers have done, I wanted to photograph the joy in their lives,” Park said. “‘Nights in Paradise’ grew out of those encounters.” “One of the friends I made among the people experiencing homelessness was gay," the photographer said. "Through him, I began visiting gay nightlife venues, where I heard many stories about love, betrayal and the judgment people faced from society. Those encounters gave shape to the project.” Over the years, Park developed friendships with the men who identified as “iban,” gradually earning their trust and gaining insights into their lives through his lens. Through this project, he hopes that visitors will meet these images with acceptance and an open mind. “In Korea, where sexual minorities struggle for social acceptance, I wanted to understand their difficulties, their experiences of love and separation, and convey something of their inner lives to the wider public with warmth and empathy,” he explained. “I also hope they see the comfort and joy these people create together.” “Nights in Paradise” is on view until Oct. 29 at Gallery Bresson in Chungmuro, while “Earthly Paradise” runs until Nov. 1 at Gallery Pohang in North Gyeongsang Province. Following these exhibitions, the series continues with “The Desire of the Horse-Headed Man.” Centered on a fictional figure Park calls the “Horse-Headed Man,” the exhibition examines humanity’s relationship with nature and the contradictions of technological progress. The work draws inspiration from Steven Spielberg’s 2001 science fiction film “A.I. Artificial Intelligence.” “The Desire of the Horse-Headed Man” will be featured at the 10th Photography Island Songdo event, which brings together 50 participating photographers. The three-day art fair will run from Oct. 30 to Nov. 1 at the Commodore Hotel Pohang. All exhibitions are free of charge. WASHINGTON — The U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has ordered federal civilian agencies to remove products developed by Chinese artificial intelligence (AI) startup DeepSeek from their information technology systems and barred them from procuring such products, according to a federal notice released Monday. The order, detailed in a notice scheduled to be published in the Federal Register on Tuesday, applies to information technology products and services developed by Hangzhou DeepSeek Artificial Intelligence Co. and its affiliated entities. The restrictions also cover third-party products and services developed using DeepSeek implementations. The department said the order was issued under the Federal Acquisition Supply Chain Security Act of 2018 following a review of a recommendation by the Federal Acquisition Security Council and related evidence. The order applies to federal civilian agency IT systems and procurements, rather than imposing a general ban on the use of DeepSeek products by private businesses or individuals in the United States. TEL AVIV — In Hungary’s general election in April, Prime Minister Viktor Orbán’s right-wing populist government was toppled not by some leftist opposition, but rather by a center-right party committed to fighting corruption and restoring democracy. As Israel heads to the polls on Oct. 27, a similar shift is by far the best outcome one can reasonably hope for, with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s extremist government replaced by a decent, law-abiding administration. A radically new foreign policy will remain out of reach. In a “normal” democracy, a leader like Netanyahu would have been forced to resign or toppled by popular protests long ago. After all, it was under his watch that Israel endured the horrific terrorist attack of Oct. 7, 2023, and under his orders that Israel has undertaken multiple prolonged wars — marked by war crimes — which exhausted its capacities and alienated the international community. But Israel is not a normal democracy, and its voters have never been particularly concerned about accountability. While Netanyahu does not command broad-based support — polls largely rule out the possibility that his bloc will retain a majority — his defeat is far from guaranteed. This has little to do with policy: while liberals sometimes present programs and proposals, Israeli elections have always been less about policy platforms than about culture and tribal identity. Netanyahu bears no small share of responsibility for this. For decades, he has won support by pitting two competing concepts of identity — Israeli-ness and Jewishness — against each other. He has played on people’s fears, recalling episodes of Arab hostility and Palestinian intifadas, while promoting the idea that there is no peaceful route to Israeli security. Even the West, he says, is fundamentally antisemitic: it will always end up putting the Jews in the dock. But Netanyahu’s focus is never on a secure future; it is on the catastrophe that supposedly lies just around the corner. The Oct. 7 massacre, and the world’s “hypocritical” opprobrium over Israel’s subsequent war of “self-defense,” seemed, to many, to vindicate Netanyahu’s narrative. Nonetheless, years of war, political corruption, and democratic erosion under Netanyahu’s leadership have alienated some elements of Israel’s electorate. But such voters have not been absorbed by a cohesive opposition. Instead, they have found an amalgam of right-wing parties, center-right and center-left formations, and only one clearly left-wing party, Yair Golan’s Democrats. The opposition parties are united by a few objectives. They want to hold Netanyahu accountable for the security failures that made the Oct. 7 attack possible and for the conduct of the war in Gaza. They want to halt his anti-democratic judicial reforms. And they want to force the large ultra-Orthodox community — a key partner in Netanyahu’s governments—to share the burden of military service (from which they are exempt) and to participate in the labor market (instead of living on government subsidies). This platform is unlikely to attract a clear majority. Instead, polls now point to a tie between the two major blocs. And whereas Netanyahu is an unscrupulous campaigner, who would stop at nothing to build a coalition that keeps him in power, the opposition parties have pledged not to coalesce with “non-Zionist” forces. This puts the opposition in a quandary, as their only real chance of forming a government would involve a deal with the Arab parties. One alternative could be to form a minority government with the Arab parties’ tacit support, undo some of Netanyahu’s anti-democratic legislation, and then call a snap election to gain more legitimacy. There is also a scenario where the two competing blocs employ an odd Israeli political invention, forming a grand coalition with two prime ministers rotating at the head of the government.

The successful trial voyage of the PanStar Acro container ship from Busan to Felixstowe in the United Kingdom and back has attracted national and international attention. Completing the round trip in just 50 days, the vessel demonstrated the potential of the Northern Sea Route (NSR) as a new shipping corridor for Korea. The ship departed from Busan on Aug. 22 and arrived in Felixstowe on Sept. 12, taking only 20 days and seven hours for the outbound voyage. This achievement highlights new possibilities for Korea’s maritime trade and logistics industry and underscores the need for proactive preparation as the route gains strategic importance. The NSR is the shortest maritime route between Asia and Europe via the Arctic Ocean. Compared with the Suez Canal route, it reduces distance by about 7,000km, shortens transit time by 10 days and cuts shipping costs by roughly 30 percent. Interest in the NSR has existed for decades. However, commercial use has remained limited due to extreme weather, ice-covered waters, insufficient infrastructure and weak emergency response capabilities. It has periodically been used to transport heat-sensitive and time-critical cargoes, such as batteries, solar panels, semiconductors, pharmaceuticals and vaccines. Chinese shipping company Sea Legend operates a regular container service along the route, reflecting growing market interest. Today, climate change and geopolitical risks arising from the conflicts in the Middle East and the war in Ukraine are enhancing the strategic importance of the NSR, particularly in Asia. More governments and shipping companies are interested in the NSR as an alternative shipping corridor to mitigate geopolitical uncertainties and strengthen supply chain resilience. Climate change is causing Arctic sea ice to thin and recede. According to a 2022 study published in Communications Earth & Environment, the Arctic warmed 3.8 times faster than the global average between 1979 and 2021. In late summer, parts of the route become ice-free. These changing conditions made the PanStar Acro’s voyage possible without the assistance of an icebreaker. As the ice-free period lengthens and more ice-strengthened vessels enter service, the NSR is likely to become increasingly attractive to shippers. However, greater advances in shipbuilding, sustainable fuels, infrastructure and maritime safety are needed for the NSR to become commercially viable. Equally important will be enhanced cooperation among key stakeholders with a strong interest in secure and efficient maritime trade routes, including Russia, the United States, China, Korea, Japan, India and Singapore. Floating ice remains a major obstacle to the commercial viability of the NSR. According to the PanStar Acro's Automatic Identification System track speed profile, it encountered substantial floating ice in the Chukchi and East Siberian seas and had to halt its voyage on Sept. 1. Despite shrinking sea ice, navigation along the NSR still requires ice-strengthened vessels. Heavy fuel oil (HFO), widely used by large commercial vessels for its price competitiveness, generates significant amounts of black carbon that accumulate on Arctic ice and snow, accelerating ice melting. HFO spills can have severe environmental consequences because the fuel decomposes slowly and is difficult to remove. Also, differing geopolitical interpretations over the legal status and governance of the NSR remain a challenge that must be addressed if it is to achieve broader commercial development. Vessels transiting the route are required to obtain navigation permits from Russia’s ROSATOM and comply with its reporting requirements. However, some countries, including China, argue that the NSR should be governed by the principle of freedom of navigation under the U.N. Convention on the Law of the Sea.

Inaugural Seongbuk Art Week traces artists' lives and memories that shaped creative enclave In Seongbuk-dong, a quiet neighborhood tucked beyond Seoul’s centuries-old city wall, traditional houses and secluded gardens have long drawn generations of modern and contemporary Korean artists, poets and architects seeking space to live, work and reflect. Painters Kim Whan-ki, known for his abstract works, and Lee Jung-seop, best known for his paintings of white oxen, were among them. So it is fitting, then, that Seongbuk Art Week is taking shape here. Opening Tuesday, the inaugural art week will turn the neighborhood and surrounding district into an interconnected museum, featuring more than 40 exhibitions and projects. Organized by Seongbuk District, the Seongbuk Cultural Foundation and the Seongbuk Museum of Art, the event will also explore how attachments to places can endure across generations. At Seongbuk Museum of Art, a special exhibition brings together abstract ink painter Suh Se-ok and his son and installation artist Do Ho Suh, through their shared connection to the family’s Seongbuk-dong hanok, or traditional Korean house. For the elder Suh, who embraced the spirit of Joseon-era literati painters, home was a place for contemplating existence. His son grew up there before pursuing a nomadic life abroad and now explores home as something portable — a living entity layered with time and memory rather than a fixed address. The exhibition pairs their paintings together with the younger Suh’s new rubbing work tracing the hanok. Running his hands across its surfaces, the younger Suh reawakens memories of his father embedded in the house. “It feels somewhat moving and very new to me,” Do Ho Suh told reporters during a press preview Monday, describing the father-and-son exhibition as a “prequel” to a larger presentation he hopes to develop with the museum. While their interests overlap, he cautioned against seeing only continuity between father and son. “I think it would be right to look at both the similarities and the differences at the same time,” he said. At Seongbuk Historical and Cultural Park, sculptor Chung Hyun’s seven The Standing Man sculptures, made between 2015 and 2021, rise beneath Hanyangdoseong, Seoul’s city wall. First built in 1396, the wall bears traces of successive rebuilding campaigns in its differently sized and colored stones. Chung’s weathered railroad ties carry another history: years spent absorbing passing trains’ weight and vibration. “The railroad ties themselves are about enduring time,” Chung said, explaining why he chose the site. “They are about enduring hardship.” The wall’s protective role and the wood’s long endurance, he said, bring the two materials into conversation. At Seongbuk-dong Byeolseo, a traditional garden created by late-Joseon official and writer Hwang Yun-myeong, Han Sung-pil addresses a more recent wound. Designated a scenic site in 2020, the garden temporarily opens for the festival. Its Songseokjeong pavilion was partially destroyed by fire in 2025. Han’s “Songseokjeong: Built of Emptiness” reconstructs its appearance on a protective screen through an ink-and-color painting based on documentary photographs. “Drawing is building,” the artist said. The image restores the missing pavilion to the landscape while the building awaits restoration. At Simujang, where poet and independence activist Han Yong-un lived from 1933 until his final years, Lee Woo-sung brings contemporary painting into a home associated with literature and resistance. The house’s name invokes the Buddhist search for a lost ox, a metaphor for seeking enlightenment. Lee reinterprets that journey in “Searching for the Ox,” while “To Live With a Singing Heart” brings animals and a guitar into the grounds, imagining music accompanying the aspirations preserved there.

Trump signed the legislation after both chambers of Congress approved it, only to retreat from its central objective now.
Washington is becoming a theatre of political contradictions. Lindsey Graham spent two years pushing for tougher measures against Russia, arguing that cutting Moscow’s oil revenue was essential to ending the Ukraine war. Yet his proposed 100% tariffs on India and China risked disrupting global trade, raising consumer prices and wrecking decades of economic integration. China would have borne the greatest impact, potentially derailing efforts to stabilize U.S.–China trade. India, too, would have suffered unnecessarily.

Russia, China, India and the wider global economy can breathe a little easier. Supporters of Graham’s legislation may protest Trump’s willingness to resume Russian fuel imports, but the administration faces a choice between ideological posturing and practical necessity.
Trump has chosen necessity—for now. The episode exposes the weakness of a policy that threatens sweeping economic punishment without adequately considering its consequences.

The AES Effect documents the most significant shift in West African geopolitics since independence. For decades, the Sahel provided the raw materials for Europe. Niger’s uranium lit the streets of Paris while the people of Niger sat in darkness and suffered the effects of radiation contamination in their air and water. Switzerland refined Mali’s and Burkina Faso’s gold and European textile mills processed their cotton for international markets while Burkinabès and Malians lived in squalor.

Since NATO bombed Libya, ISIS-aligned terrorist groups have been taking over the Sahel. Through a succession of coups in 2021, 2022 and 2023, General Assimi Goïta, Captain Ibrahim Traoré and General Abdourahamane Tchiani took power, expelled foreign troops, and formed a military and economic alliance to fight terrorism and reclaim the Sahel for the people.

Mali and Burkina Faso nationalized their gold. Niger took back its uranium. Burkina Faso is spinning its own cotton, processing its own tomatoes, and has opened its first gold refinery.

Despite sanctions, demands from the European Union, media smears, coordinated terrorist attacks and assassination attempts, the Alliance of Sahel States is still standing. Other African leaders are watching, and some are joining the wave of resource nationalization to break the chains of neocolonialism.

Some call Ibrahim Traoré a cult of personality or a demagogue. They call the transitional presidents junta leaders. What are the facts on the ground? How far will this movement spread?

The Center for Political Innovation stands firmly behind the Alliance of Sahel States. As the Imperialist/Globalist economic system run by Wall Street and London crumbles, a multipolar world is rising based on win-win trade and development. African liberation is a key pillar in this rising economy.
